title: The Cartomancer's Debt
summary: A fortune-teller in the night market reads your future for free — but each reading quietly takes a memory in payment. When Sable trades away too much to learn how her story ends, she has to decide whether a future is worth having if you forget everything that led you there.

chapters.title: Free of Charge
chapters.body:
The night market of Lowlamp only sold things you couldn't hold. Bottled courage for a hard conversation. An hour of forgetting, for grief too fresh to carry. A stranger's good luck, secondhand and slightly worn. Sable had walked its crooked aisles a hundred times without buying anything, because her mother had taught her the market's one law: nothing there is really free, and the things that look free cost the most.

But Sable was thirteen, and thirteen is an age full of questions about how things will turn out, and at the far end of the market, under a torn red awning, sat a woman who promised answers.

The sign said: YOUR FUTURE, READ TRUE. NO CHARGE.

The woman was neither old nor young. She had a deck of cards worn soft as cloth, and eyes that seemed to look slightly past you, at something just over your shoulder. She smiled when Sable slowed, and gestured to the empty stool across her little table.

"You have a question," the cartomancer said. It wasn't a guess. "Everyone who slows down here has the same one, in the end. How does it turn out? Will it be all right?" She spread the soft cards face-down in a fan. "Sit. I'll show you. No charge."

"Nothing here is free," said Sable, repeating her mother.

The cartomancer's smile widened, pleased, as if Sable had passed a small test. "Clever girl. You're right. But the price isn't coins." She tapped the cards. "When I read your future, the reading takes a little something in payment. A memory. Just one, and only a small one — the older, the fainter, the better. You won't even miss it. Nobody misses the memories they've already half-forgotten." She leaned back. "A morning you don't remember anyway. The taste of a meal from years ago. The face of someone you met once. In exchange, you get to see how your story turns out. Most people think that's a bargain. And most people are happy to pay."

Sable should have stood up. But she had a question that had been keeping her awake — a real one, about her sick father and the family's dwindling money and whether any of it would ever be all right — and the promise of an answer pulled at her like a hand on her sleeve.

"Just one small memory?" she asked. "And I'd forget one I didn't even want?"

"Just one," said the cartomancer softly, already beginning to turn the first card. "You'll never know it's gone.

chapters.title: One Small Memory
chapters.body:
The first reading cost Sable the smell of her grandmother's kitchen.

She didn't notice it go. The cartomancer turned three soft cards, murmured about a hard winter that would pass, about a door opening where a window closed, and Sable walked home lighter and hopeful — and if someone had asked her, that night, what her grandmother's kitchen used to smell like, she would have frowned and found only a blank, and thought nothing of it. You don't miss what you can't remember missing.

But the readings, like all easy things, were easy to want again.

The first answer had been vague — doors and windows, winters that pass. Sable wanted more. She wanted specifics. Would her father get better? Would the money come? Would she have to leave school? So she went back. And back. And each time, the cartomancer turned the soft cards and gave her a little more of the future, and each time, a memory paid the fare.

The sound of her father's laugh, from before he got sick. Gone. The name of her first friend. Gone. The color of the dress she'd worn to her aunt's wedding, and the wedding itself, and the aunt. Gone, gone, gone. The cartomancer had been honest in a way — she took the old and faint ones first, the ones already fading. But there are only so many faint memories in a young life, and once those are spent, the readings begin to take the bright ones.

Sable started to notice, at last, when the gaps got big enough to trip on.

She'd be walking home and realize she couldn't remember the way she'd come. She'd look at her father's face and feel, for one horrible second, that she wasn't quite sure who he was, before the feeling passed. She caught herself in the market one evening unable to remember why she'd come, or what her own question had been — the question, the one about her father, the one that had started all of it. She knew there had been a question. She just couldn't find it anymore.

And the future the cartomancer showed her got clearer and clearer, in exact proportion to how blurry her past became. Sable could see, now, in the soft cards, precisely how her story would turn out — every turn of it laid bare. But she was becoming a girl with a vivid future and no past, a story with an ending and no beginning, a person walking forward into a bright clear tomorrow while everything behind her dissolved into fog.

One night she sat down at the little table, and the cartomancer fanned the cards, and Sable opened her mouth to ask her question — and couldn't remember it. Couldn't remember her father was sick. Couldn't remember she had a father. Could remember nothing but the market, and the cards, and the hunger to see more.

"One more reading," the cartomancer said gently, "and I can show you the very end. The last card. How it all finishes. Wouldn't you like to know how it all finishes?"

And Sable, hollow and forgetting, almost said yes. Almost paid the last bright memory she had left to learn the ending of a story she could no longer remember living.

chapters.title: The Story You Live
chapters.body:
Sable's hand was halfway to the cards when a small thing stopped her.

In her pocket, her fingers brushed something — a pressed flower, dry and brittle, that she didn't remember picking. But her hand remembered. Her hand knew to be gentle with it. And though her mind had lost the memory, her body had kept the shape of it: someone had given her this flower, someone she'd loved, on a day that had mattered. She couldn't recall who, or when, or why. But she could feel, holding it, the shape of the loving. The proof that there had been a past worth having, even if she could no longer see it.

And something surfaced in her — not a memory, because those were spent, but something deeper, a thing the cartomancer's cards had never been able to touch. Her mother's one law. Nothing here is free, and the things that look free cost the most.

Sable looked at the cartomancer, at the eyes that looked just past her, at the soft cards fanned and waiting. And she understood, all at once, what she had done. She had been trading away the story she had lived to buy the story she hadn't lived yet. And a future, she realized — however clear, however bright — is worth nothing if you've forgotten everything that made you want it. What good is knowing how your story ends if you can't remember why you cared how it ends? An ending only means something because of everything that came before it. Strip away the before, and the ending is just a fact about a stranger.

"No," Sable said, and pulled her hand back from the cards.

The cartomancer's past-looking eyes focused, for the first time, directly on her. "No? But you're so close. One more, and you'll know everything. How it all turns out. Isn't that what you came for?"

"I don't even remember what I came for," said Sable, and her voice shook, because it was a terrible thing to admit. "I traded it away. I traded away my grandmother's kitchen and my friend's name and — and things I can't even name anymore, because they're gone. I've been buying my future by burning my past. And a future's no good if there's no one left inside it who remembers being me." She stood, gripping the dry flower. "I don't want to know how it ends. I want to go back and live it. Even the hard parts. Even the parts where I don't know what happens next. That's what a life is — not knowing, and living it anyway."

The cartomancer was quiet for a long moment. And then she did something Sable didn't expect: she gathered the soft cards, and set them aside, and folded her hands.

"Almost no one says no," she said, and there was something in her voice that might have been respect, or might have been grief. "They always want to see the end. They'll give me everything — every memory they have — to see the end. And they walk away with a perfect knowledge of a future they can no longer feel, forgetting even to be sad about what they lost." She looked at Sable. "You can't have back what you already spent. I want you to understand that. Your grandmother's kitchen, your friend's name — those are gone; I can't return them. The market doesn't run backward."

"I know," said Sable. And it hurt, knowing it. "But I can stop spending. I can keep what's left. And I can make new ones — a whole life of new ones — starting tonight."

She turned and walked out of the night market of Lowlamp, past the bottled courage and the secondhand luck, out into the ordinary dark, holding a dry flower she couldn't place but somehow loved. And she walked home the long way — not because she remembered it, but because she wanted to learn it again.

Her father was awake when she got home, thin and tired but smiling to see her, and when he said her name, she held onto the sound of it fiercely, the way you hold a thing you've decided never to trade away. She still didn't know how her story would turn out. Her father might get better; he might not. The money might come; it might not. The future stayed dark and uncertain in front of her, unread, unpaid-for, hers.

And Sable found, to her surprise, that she preferred it that way. Because a future you can't see is a future you get to live — one uncertain, unforgettable day at a time. And that, she understood now, was worth more than all the endings in all the cards in all the night markets in the world.
